title: Fitbit Sense ECG detection leading to diagnosis and treatment of ventricular tachycardia
summary: A Fitbit Sense watch detected an irregular heart rate of 164 beats per minute in a man in Jamshedpur, India, who sought care and was treated for ventricular tachycardia.
account: On 11 September 2020 the U.S. Food and Drug Administration cleared the Fitbit electrocardiogram (ECG) app for the detection of atrial fibrillation or sinus rhythm only. Fitbit's own summary says that this detection is not recommended for people with other known arrhythmias. By 28 September 2021 Fitbit's product page listed India among the countries where the Sense could run the ECG app. In October 2021 a 55-year-old man in Jamshedpur, India, had palpitations, sweating, anxiety and mild dizziness for half an hour while at work. His Fitbit Sense watch detected an irregular heart rate of 164 beats per minute with irregular rhythm and bizarre QRS morphology. He felt the need to visit a doctor immediately and sought care at Tata Main Hospital. A 12-lead ECG showed tachycardia at 166 beats per minute with bizarre QRS complexes under 130 milliseconds and right axis deviation. Idiopathic fascicular ventricular tachycardia was diagnosed. After adenosine did not reverse the tachycardia, clinicians restored sinus rhythm through electrical cardioversion. They also corrected severe hypokalemia with intravenous potassium. Holter monitoring, echocardiography and coronary angiography excluded structural heart disease. He subsequently received oral verapamil and telmisartan. After four cardiology visits he was reported to be doing well with no further complaints. A case report published in Cureus on 18 July 2023 describes the case and does not give the exact day of the presentation.
purpose: The Fitbit Sense ECG app records a single-lead electrocardiogram to assess heart rhythm, and its clearance covers atrial fibrillation. Capturing an abnormal rhythm for medical review was its purpose. Ventricular tachycardia lies outside the rhythms that it was cleared to classify.
system: Fitbit Sense ECG app and heart-rate monitoring

ratings.reason: The man had ventricular tachycardia at 166 beats per minute, which clinicians ended with electrical cardioversion. On verapamil he had no further complaints over four cardiology visits, so the case report describes a restored rhythm and a controlled condition.

ai_role.statement: The watch's rhythm analysis flagged an irregular 164 bpm rhythm with abnormal QRS morphology, which sent the patient to hospital. The diagnosis and treatment were made by cardiologists from a 12-lead ECG and further tests.

brief: In October 2021 a 55-year-old man in Jamshedpur, India, had symptoms at work, and his Fitbit Sense showed an irregular rhythm at 164 beats per minute. He felt the need to visit a doctor immediately and went to Tata Main Hospital, where cardiologists diagnosed idiopathic fascicular ventricular tachycardia from a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) and further tests. They restored sinus rhythm by electrical cardioversion, and on verapamil he was later reported to be doing well.[1] The U.S. Food and Drug Administration cleared the watch's ECG app to tell atrial fibrillation from sinus rhythm, and ventricular tachycardia lies outside the rhythms that it was cleared to classify.[2] The benefit also rests on an assumption that he would have waited longer without the reading, and a single case report gives no way to check it.
